definition: The whole group of people or things that a statistical question is about.
The part of a population that data is actually collected from, used to draw conclusions about the whole population.
A sample chosen so that every member of the population has the same chance of being selected.
Data that can take only separate values, usually counts, such as the number of goals in a match.
Measured data that can take any value in a range, such as a time or a mass, even when it is recorded rounded.

A built-in tendency of a sampling method to include some kinds of member of the population more often than others, so the sample misrepresents the population; a bigger sample chosen the same way does not remove it.
A data value less than $Q_{1} - 1.5 \times \mathrm{IQR}$ or greater than $Q_{3} + 1.5 \times \mathrm{IQR}$; some outliers are valid data and some are errors, so check the context before removing one.

One of the values that split ordered data into quarters: about a quarter of the data lies below the lower quartile $Q_{1}$ and about three quarters below the upper quartile $Q_{3}$; methods differ, so a GDC and a hand method can give slightly different values.
The difference between the upper and lower quartiles, $\mathrm{IQR} = Q_{3} - Q_{1}$, which measures the spread of the middle half of the data.
Choosing a sample so that every possible group of the required size is equally likely, for example by picking numbers at random from a full list of the population.
Choosing the members of the population that are easiest to reach, such as the first people you meet; it is quick but likely to be biased.

Choosing every $k$th member of an ordered list of the population, where $k = \frac{N}{n}$ (rounded down if not whole) for a population of $N$ and a sample of $n$, starting from a member picked at random among the first $k$ and stopping once there are $n$. If $n$ doesn't divide $N$, the last members of the list can never be picked.
Fixing how many members to take from each group, then letting the collector choose anyone who fits until each quota is filled; it is not random, so it can be biased.

Splitting the population into groups that share a feature, then taking a random sample from each group in proportion to its size, with the rounded group sizes adjusted so they add up to the total sample size.
